newsitem.title: UK: Strong Brent cuts W. African crude sales to Asia.
newsitem.headline: Strong Brent cuts W. African crude sales to Asia.

text.p: West African oil producers will export 250,000-300,000 barrels per day (bpd) in October to customers in Asia, traders said on Friday.

October exports are expected to total about 250,000 bpd fewer than in September, mainly because of an unattractive spread between Brent, against which most West African spot sales are priced, and Far East benchmark Dubai crude.
"The Brent-Dubai spread is extremely wide, so there is no encouragement to take barrels to the Far East," said a trader.
Brent was about $2.25 a barrel more expensive than Dubai on the forward paper markets on Friday. The Brent/Dubai spread in September has averaged about 70 cents a barrel more than in August.

The spread ballooned earlier this month as Middle East tension combined with growing concern about low northern hemisphere heating oil stocks to push benchmark Brent crude futures to a new post-Gulf War high of $24.39 a barrel.
"While the spread is not favourable at the moment, buyers like the South Koreans do need sweet crudes," said a trader.
"But when it gets to this kind of level and it doesn't make sense economically...they usually turn to Australian grades," he added.
Growing refinery capacity in the region and tighter emission standards for refined products has sparked fresh Asian demand this year for low sulphur West African barrels.
Exports peaked at a record one million barrels in February before petering out almost entirely in May and June. They recovered strongly in July to reach 800,000 bpd.
Apart from the Indian Oil Corp's regular purchase of three very large crude carriers (VLCCs) of Nigerian Qua Iboe, October exports have been limited to two VLCCs to Taiwan's CPC.

Despite the lack of an arbitrage window to the Far East and difficult economics for transatlantic sales, premiums have recovered as European and U.S. refiners scrambled for sweet, middle distillate-rich barrels like Forcados and Bonny Medium, traders said.
"There's certainly very little Nigerian crude left in October, maybe the odd Brass River, Escravos and a Qua Iboe," said a trader.
European and U.S. refiners are running at full tilt in an attempt to rebuild heating oil stocks before winter sets in. Europe is also gearing up for a switch to low sulphur diesel on October 1.
